chapterNote: The psalm of joy in the morning — David's thanksgiving after a sickness that carried him to the edge of Sheol, sung at a dedication of the house. Its shape is a rescued man's testimony with a confession folded inside it. The testimony: You drew me up like a bucket from a well, You healed me, You brought my soul back from the grave. The theology distilled from it is the verse the church has clung to at every bedside and graveside: His anger lasts a moment, His favor a lifetime; weeping may lodge for the night, but a ringing shout of joy comes with the morning. The confession is the middle: in my prosperity I said, 'I will never be shaken' — the self-assurance of the comfortable — until You hid Your face and I fell apart. Then the bargaining prayer of a dying man, honest as bone: what profit is there in my blood? Will the dust praise You? And the answer, which is the psalm's last movement: mourning turned to dancing, sackcloth stripped off and gladness belted on, all so that the glory God gave me might sing to You and never fall silent. O LORD my God, I will give thanks to You forever.

1.text: A psalm; a song for the dedication of the house. Of David. I will lift You high, O LORD, for You have drawn me up, and have not let my enemies rejoice over me.
1.amp: A Psalm [mizmor] and Song [shir] at the dedication [chanukkah] of the house [bayith] of David. I will extol [rum — exalt, raise high] You, O LORD [YHWH]; for You have lifted me up [dalah — drawn me up as a bucket from a well], and have not made my foes [oyeb] to rejoice [samach] over me.
1.notes: The superscription's chanukkah (H2598) is the dedication-word — the psalm found its liturgical home at a house-consecration, whether David's palace, the temple site, or later the rededicated temple. dalah (H1802) is the well-bucket verb: David hauled up from depth on God's rope, and rum (H7311) is the answering motion — lifted, he lifts.

2.text: O LORD my God, I cried out to You for help, and You healed me.
2.amp: O LORD [YHWH] my God [Elohim], I cried [shava — shouted for help] unto You, and You have healed [rapha] me.
2.notes: shava (H7768) is the emergency shout; rapha (H7495) the LORD's own self-title from Marah (cf. Exodus 15:26; Psalm 103:3). The verse is the whole event in two verbs — the psalm will spend the rest of its length unfolding what happened between them.

3.text: O LORD, You brought my soul up out of Sheol; You kept me alive so that I would not go down into the pit.
3.amp: O LORD [YHWH], You have brought up [alah] my soul [nephesh] from the grave [sheol]: You have kept me alive [chayah], that I should not go down [yarad] to the pit [bor].
3.notes: The illness was a descent already begun: yarad (H3381) toward the bor (H953), the cistern-grave. alah and chayah (H5927, H2421) reverse the direction — brought up, kept alive. David's near-death is testimony that God's reach extends to Sheol's doorstep (cf. Psalm 16:10).

4.text: Sing praise to the LORD, you His faithful ones, and give thanks at the remembrance of His holiness.
4.amp: Sing [zamar — make music] unto the LORD [YHWH], O ye saints [chasid — His covenant-faithful ones] of His, and give thanks [yadah] at the remembrance ['to the memorial', zeker, the KJV margin] of His holiness [qodesh].
4.notes: One man's healing conscripts the whole congregation: the chasidim (H2623) summoned to zamar. The object is zeker qodsho (H2143, H6944) — 'His holy memorial', the Name by which He is remembered (cf. Exodus 3:15): thanksgiving aimed at who He is, prompted by what He did.

5.text: For His anger lasts only a moment; His favor lasts a lifetime. Weeping may come to lodge for the night, but with the morning comes a ringing shout of joy.
5.amp: For His anger [aph] endures but a moment ['there is but a moment in his anger', rega, the KJV margin]; in His favour [ratson] is life [chay]: weeping [bechi] may endure ['in the evening', lun — lodge overnight, the KJV margin] for a night [erev], but joy ['singing', rinnah — the ringing cry, the KJV margin] comes in the morning [boqer].
5.notes: The verse generations have gripped in the dark. The proportions are the doctrine: rega (H7281), one moment, of aph — against chayyim, a whole lifetime, of ratson (H7522). And bechi (H1065) is pictured as a lodger, lun (H3885), who checks in at erev and checks out at boqer, when rinnah (H7440) arrives to take the room. Grief is real, and it is a tenant, not the owner (cf. Isaiah 54:7-8; 2 Corinthians 4:17).

6.text: As for me, in my ease I had said, 'I will never be shaken.'
6.amp: And in my prosperity [shalvah — ease, security] I said [amar], 'I shall never [olam] be moved [mot].'
6.notes: The confession inside the thanksgiving: shalvah (H7959) is untroubled ease — Psalm 73's word for the wicked's comfort, here David's own. 'Never mot' (H4131) was the right sentence with the wrong subject: true of God's kept man, false as self-assessment (cf. Deuteronomy 8:17; 1 Corinthians 10:12).

7.text: O LORD, by Your favor You had made my mountain stand strong; then You hid Your face, and I was thrown into dismay.
7.amp: LORD [YHWH], by Your favour [ratson] You had made my mountain stand strong ['settled strength for my mountain', amad oz, the KJV margin]: You did hide [satar] Your face [panim], and I was troubled [bahal — dismayed, panicked].
7.notes: The diagnosis of verse 6: the har stood by ratson (H7522), God's favor — never by David's own footing. One satar panim (H5641, H6440), the hidden face, and bahal (H926), panic: the man who would 'never be moved' discovered his mountain was borrowed.

8.text: To You, O LORD, I called, and to the Lord I made my plea for grace:
8.amp: I cried [qara] to You, O LORD [YHWH]; and unto the LORD I made supplication [chanan — pleaded for grace].
8.notes: The sickness did what prosperity never did: qara (H7121), the call, and chanan (H2603), the grace-plea — the same root as the chen God gives. The verses that follow quote the prayer verbatim, including its rough edges.

9.text: 'What gain is there in my blood, in my going down to the pit? Can dust give You thanks? Can it tell of Your faithfulness?
9.amp: 'What profit [betsa] is there in my blood [dam], when I go down [yarad] to the pit [shachat]? Shall the dust [afar] praise [yadah] You? shall it declare [nagad] Your truth [emeth]?'
9.notes: A dying man's negotiation, and God kept it in the canon: betsa (H1215), profit — what does heaven GAIN by my death? The argument is worship-economics: afar (H6083) cannot yadah, cannot nagad emeth. Hezekiah prayed the same logic and got fifteen years (cf. Isaiah 38:18-19) — God apparently honors the plea that His praise would lose a voice.

10.text: Listen, O LORD, and show me grace; O LORD, come and be my help!'
10.amp: 'Hear [shama], O LORD [YHWH], and have mercy [chanan] upon me: LORD, be You my helper [azar].'
10.notes: The negotiation ends where all real prayer ends — in three imperatives with no leverage left: shama, chanan, azar (H8085, H2603, H5826). Hear, be gracious, help. The bargaining gives way to begging, and begging is answered.

11.text: You have turned my mourning into dancing for me; You have untied my sackcloth and belted me with gladness,
11.amp: You have turned [haphak — overturned, transformed] for me my mourning [misped] into dancing [machol]: You have put off [pathach — loosed, opened] my sackcloth [saq], and girded [azar — belted] me with gladness [simchah];
11.notes: haphak (H2015) is total reversal, the verb of Psalm 32:4 now running the other way: misped (H4553), the funeral wail, into machol (H4234), the circle-dance. God works as a dresser — pathach (H6605) the sackcloth's knot, azar (H247) the belt of simchah — the whole wardrobe of grief exchanged (cf. Isaiah 61:3).

12.text: so that my glory might sing praise to You and never fall silent. O LORD my God, I will give You thanks forever.
12.amp: To the end that my glory [kabod — 'my tongue, or, my soul', the KJV margin] may sing [zamar] praise to You, and not be silent [damam]: O LORD [YHWH] my God [Elohim], I will give thanks [yadah] unto You for ever [olam].
12.notes: The purpose clause answers verse 9's question: the dust would have been silent — damam (H1826) — so God kept a kabod (H3519), a glory-with-a-tongue, alive to zamar. Every rescue is a voice retained for the choir; and David signs the contract: yadah le-olam, thanks without a term.
